Segmented-with-Jump Term: Slope and Level Both Changing

Source: R/segmented.R
jseg.Rd

jseg() specifies a covariate whose slope and level both change at \(K\) break-points estimated with everything else, and the term is the union of seg() and jump() at the same points. Written in the equation of any parameter of any distribution, the term contributes

$$\beta x_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \bigl[\delta_k\,\mathbb{1}(x_i \geq \psi_k) + \gamma_k\,(x_i - \psi_k)_{+}\bigr]$$

to that parameter's linear predictor, so that in a model \(g(\theta_i) = \eta_i\) in which the rest of the equation supplies \(z_i'\alpha\),

$$\eta_i = z_i'\alpha + \beta x_i + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \bigl[\delta_k\,\mathbb{1}(x_i \geq \psi_k) + \gamma_k\,(x_i - \psi_k)_{+}\bigr].$$

\(\beta\) is the slope before the first break-point, \(\gamma_k\) the change of slope at \(\psi_k\) and \(\delta_k\) the change of level there.

Usage

jseg(
  x,
  ...,
  npsi = 1,
  psi = NULL,
  by = NULL,
  linear = TRUE,
  c0 = 0.05,
  smoothed = NULL,
  marginal = FALSE,
  n_boot = 10,
  label = "jseg"
)

Arguments

x

The covariate, an expression evaluated in the data.

...

Two-sided formulas developing the term's own coefficients; see the section above. Cannot be combined with by.

npsi

The number of break-points. Defaults to 1.

psi

Optional starting positions; defaults to evenly spaced quantiles of the covariate. Where a break-point carries a development, they seed it, and each starting vector solves \(Wp_k \approx \psi_k^{0}\).

by

A one-sided formula giving every coefficient of the term the same development, e.g. by = ~0 + g for an independent set per level of a factor. A bare variable is rejected; write the formula.

linear

Whether the block carries the linear effect \(\beta x\). Defaults to TRUE.

c0

The starting value of the scaling factor that separates the observations from the break-point, as a fraction of the distance to the ends of the range. Defaults to 0.05, the value that Fasola et al. (2018) recommend; see Details.

smoothed

NULL (the default: the construction exactly as documented above) or a numericals7 numericals7::abs_smoother(), e.g. numericals7::smooth_probit(). The smoother replaces the step and the hinge by their smooth versions, \((1 + s'(u))/2\) and \((u + s(u))/2\), so every break-point becomes an ordinary parameter of a model as smooth as the smoother (\(C^\infty\) for the probit and the hyperbolic, \(C^3\) for the quintic; the page of the quintic gives its cost under an outer criterion, where the probit is the recommended smoother). There is no working parametrization, no auxiliary coefficient and no scaling schedule (for jump() and jseg(), a c0 that is passed is ignored with a message). The block is the true Jacobian and the term is fitted by Gauss-Newton like nl(). A smoothed term accepts a development of any coefficient, including a break-point (psi ~ random(~1 | id)) and penalized developments, for every kind, since a smoothed term has no read-off that would constrain the development. The smoother's width is resolved at build from the covariate's spacing (the median gap between distinct values, within groups where a break-point development supplies a partition) unless the object carries one. For the quintic, which is exact outside its width, the width is raised to at least 0.55 times the largest gap over the range that a break-point may take, so that a break-point cannot sit in a gap with no observation within its width. The width is reported: it is the width of the transition (the bent-cable reading). The smoothing bias is zero outside the transition for the quintic, decays with the Gaussian tails for the probit, and decays as \(c/(4|u|)\) for the hyperbolic, whose parameter \(c\) is a squared length. The objective remains multimodal in the positions: smoothing rounds the local optima and does not remove them, so the profile start and the n_boot restarts remain necessary.

marginal

Whether the break-point is a latent variable per group, integrated out of the likelihood exactly instead of being an estimated position. FALSE, the default, is the construction documented above. TRUE requires the subformula psi ~ random(~1 | g) and returns a structural term of the likelihood shape (MarginalBreakTerm()); see the section on the marginal construction in jump(). For a seg term the native random-changepoint fit (psi ~ random(~1 | g) without marginal) estimates the break-points as the mode of the latent distribution and is the recommended route, while the marginal construction is the exact-likelihood alternative. The marginal seg has one break-point: the conditional is smooth in the position, so the integral runs on Gauss-Kronrod panels over the intervals between a group's ordered observations, and several latent break-points would need a product quadrature with a number of components that a fitting layer cannot carry.

n_boot

How many bootstrap restarts the fitting layer runs after the iteration first converges (Wood 2001, the device that segmented runs by default): each restart re-estimates on a bootstrap resample from the current break-points and then on the data again from where the resample ended, keeping the better fit. The objective has local optima in the break-points, and with several of them a grid start does not reach the right basin from every placement. Defaults to 10, segmented's own default; 0 disables. The term itself only declares the value; running the restarts is the fitting layer's, as with a penalty's hyperparameters.

label

A single non-empty string prefixed to the coefficient names.

Value

An object of class SegTerm() (a specification; see term_build()), or of class MarginalBreakTerm() with marginal = TRUE.

Details

Both devices of the two constructions are used at once: the truncated line is differentiable in the break-point and the step is linearized by the identity of Fasola et al. (2018), on the rescaled covariate that its scaling schedule provides (see jump()). The read-off is particular to the joint term, because the truncated line depends on the break-point as well, and a read-off from only the step's pair would discard the information that the change of slope carries about the break-point. Linearizing both parts about the previous position, and writing \(h\) for the increment, \(U\) for the truncated line and \(I = Z - \psi^{0}W\) for the indicator,

$$\gamma\,(x-\psi)_{+} \approx \gamma U - \gamma h I, \qquad \delta\,\mathbb{1}(x>\psi) = \delta Z - \delta\psi W,$$

so the fitted coefficients of \(Z\) and \(W\) are \(a = \delta - \gamma h\) and \(b = \gamma h\psi^{0} - \delta\psi^{0} - \delta h\), and the increment solves

$$\gamma h^{2} + a h + (b + a\psi^{0}) = 0,$$

the root of smaller modulus. At \(\gamma = 0\) the quadratic degenerates to \(h = -(b + a\psi^{0})/a\), that is \(\psi = -b/a\), so the pure step is a special case of this reading.

Everything that jump() documents about the scaling schedule, the confinement of a break-point and the choice of starting positions applies here unchanged.

The coefficients

The coefficients are beta (present when linear = TRUE), gamma1 ... gammaK, the changes of slope, then delta1 ... deltaK, the changes of level, then g1 ... gK, the auxiliary coefficients from which the break-points are read; seg_psi() reports the break-points. A smoothed term holds the break-points directly, and its coefficients end with psi1 ... psiK in place of g1 ... gK.

Developing a coefficient with covariates

beta enters the block linearly and takes a development on any design. gammaK, deltaK and psiK all enter the quadratic above, which is a scalar identity: it splits observation by observation only where the design has one column per group and each observation belongs to one. A sharp jseg therefore accepts a development of these coefficients when each one that varies (a development with a single column is a scalar) carries the same development, the break-point is among them, and the design partitions the rows, as by = ~0 + g gives: jseg(x, by = ~0 + g) is an independent set of everything per level. Any other development of gamma, delta or psi is rejected. The componentwise reading that would remain diverges whenever a change of level passes near zero during the iteration, which happens routinely in a joint model, and for that reason the development is rejected. A smoothed jseg accepts a development of any coefficient.

The marginal construction

jseg(x, psi ~ random(~1 | g), marginal = TRUE) integrates a latent break-point per group out of the likelihood exactly, on the Gauss-Kronrod panels of seg()'s marginal, where the change of level enters each interval's conditional as a constant. The mode-based routes approximate the integral over the latent break-points by a Laplace approximation, and the marginal construction evaluates it by quadrature.

References

Muggeo, V. M. R. (2003). Estimating regression models with unknown break-points. Statistics in Medicine, 22(19), 3055–3071.

Fasola, S., Muggeo, V. M. R. and Kuchenhoff, H. (2018). A heuristic, iterative algorithm for change-point detection in abrupt change models. Computational Statistics, 33, 997–1015.

See also

seg(), jump(), seg_psi(), seg_start(), seg_step()

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(200, 0, 10)))
dd$y <- 1 + 0.3 * dd$x + 2 * (dd$x > 6) +
  1.5 * pmax(dd$x - 6, 0) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)

built <- term_build(jseg(x), dd)
term_coef_names(built)
#> [1] "jseg.beta"   "jseg.gamma1" "jseg.delta1" "jseg.g1"    


# The term is fitted next. The data are simulated from a known truth, so the
# estimates below can be read against it.
if (requireNamespace("statmodels7", quietly = TRUE)) {
  set.seed(3)
  fd <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(300, 0, 10)))
  fd$y <- 1 + 0.3 * fd$x + 1.5 * (fd$x > 6) + 1.2 * pmax(fd$x - 6, 0) +
    rnorm(300, sd = 0.3)
  ft <- statmodels7::statmod(y ~ jseg(x),
                             distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), fd)
  # The truth is intercept 1, slope 0.3, and at 6 a jump of 1.5 with a
  # change of slope of 1.2.
  round(coef(ft)$mu, 2)
}
#> (Intercept)   jseg.beta jseg.gamma1 jseg.delta1   jseg.psi1 
#>        1.08        0.28        1.19        1.62        6.00
